**Distance** is the total area under the v-t graph counted as **positive throughout**,
even where the velocity is negative.
**Step 1 — read the graph in five pieces.**
**0 to 2 s**: v rises from 0 to 4 m s⁻¹ - a triangle
**2 to 3 s**: v constant at 4 m s⁻¹ - a rectangle
**3 to 4·333 s**: v falls from 4 to 0 at S - a triangle
**4·333 to 5 s**: v falls on to −2 m s⁻¹ at C - a triangle **below** the axis
**5 to 6 s**: v returns from −2 to 0 at D - another triangle below the axis
**Step 2 — find each area.**
½(2)(4) = **4 m**
(1)(4) = **4 m**
½(1·333)(4) = **2·667 m**
½(0·667)(2) = **0·667 m**
½(1)(2) = **1 m**
**Step 3 — add them all as positive quantities.**
4 + 4 + 2·667 + 0·667 + 1 = **12·333 m = 37/3 m** ✓
**Why the straight line BC gives those two sub-triangles.** The line falls from 4 m s⁻¹
at t = 3 and crosses zero at S = 4·333 s, so its slope is −4/1·333 = **−3 m s⁻²** ✓
Continuing at that slope to t = 5 gives v = −3(5 − 4·333) = **−2 m s⁻¹**, which is point
C as drawn - confirming the reading of the graph.
**Distance against displacement.** Counting the last two areas as **negative** instead
gives the **displacement**:
4 + 4 + 2·667 − 0·667 − 1 = **9 m**
The body went 10·667 m forward, then came back 1·667 m ✓ Distance is 12·333 m,
displacement 9 m, and the question asks for the first.
**Why the exact answer is a fraction.** With S at 13/3 seconds, the two sub-triangles
have areas 2/3 and ... in exact form:
3 to 13/3: ½(4/3)(4) = **8/3**
13/3 to 5: ½(2/3)(2) = **2/3**
total: 4 + 4 + 8/3 + 2/3 + 1 = 9 + 10/3 = **37/3 m** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **12 m** ✗ and **11 m** ✗ are near misses that drop one of
the small triangles. **49/4 m = 12·25 m** ✗ is close but corresponds to S at a slightly
different time ✓ The 4·333 s is given precisely so the fractions come out exact.
∴ (37/3) m.

Position is the **area under the velocity-time graph**, so read the graph in blocks up to
t = 5 s.
**Step 1 — read the graph from 0 to 5 s.**
**0 to 2 s**: v rises linearly from 0 to 2 m s⁻¹
**2 to 4 s**: v constant at 2 m s⁻¹
**4 to 5 s**: v constant at 3 m s⁻¹
**Step 2 — find each area.**
triangle, 0 to 2 s: ½(2)(2) = **2 m**
rectangle, 2 to 4 s: (2)(2) = **4 m**
rectangle, 4 to 5 s: (1)(3) = **3 m**
**Step 3 — add.**
x = 2 + 4 + 3
= **9 m** ✓
**Why area gives position here.** The particle starts at the **origin** and the velocity
is **positive throughout**, so it only ever moves forward ✓ Displacement, distance and
position are all the same number, and each equals the area under the curve.
**Why the area rule works.** Over a short interval dt the particle moves v dt, which is
the area of a thin strip ✓ Adding the strips - that is, integrating - gives the total
displacement, and for straight-line graphs the integral is just triangles and rectangles.
**A check by stages.**
at t = 2 s: x = **2 m**
at t = 4 s: x = 2 + 4 = **6 m**
at t = 5 s: x = 6 + 3 = **9 m** ✓
and the particle is still speeding away at 3 m s⁻¹ at that moment.
**Where the distractors come from.** **6 m** ✗ is the position at t = 4 s - stopping one
block short. **3 m** ✗ is the last block alone. **10 m** ✗ counts the 0 to 2 s ramp as a
full rectangle (2 x 2 = 4 instead of 2) ✓ The triangle is the piece most often
mishandled.
**Reading the first block carefully.** From 0 to 2 s the graph is a **sloping line**, so
the area is ½ base x height = **2 m**, not 4 m ✓ Treating a ramp as a rectangle is the
single commonest error in graph questions of this kind.
∴ 9 m.
